content.text:
Plan a story of about 2500 words from this premise.

Write a extremely scary ghost story in the first person, with clear logic and engaging content. Approximately 2500 words.

Propose about 4 scenes of roughly 625 words each. Give every character, location and significant object a stable id now — later scenes can only refer to entities that exist. State the world rules the story must not break. Then call submit_plan.

entities.sketch: The narrator and viewpoint character. Late thirties, returned to her childhood house to settle her recently deceased mother's estate. Practical, grieving, skeptical of superstition but emotionally fragile.

Evie Ashford, the ghost. A girl who died decades ago; her presence is tethered to a small brass locket and to reflections in a particular walnut mirror. She remembers being seen and named, and she demands witnesses.

The Ashford family home: a tired Victorian on the edge of a marsh. It smells of damp wood and old books; the house has an attic, a long hallway with mirrors, and windows that look out onto reeds and mudflats.

The locked, dustless attic of the Ashford house. Under rafters and oilcloth, trunks and trunks of forgotten things accumulate. The walnut mirror and a trunk with the locket and the faded photograph are stored here.
A tall, walnut-framed, full-length mirror with a slight warp in the glass. It never gathers dust on its surface and its reflection sometimes shows the attic as it was decades earlier.
A small, tarnished brass locket on a fragile chain. Inside is a tiny sepia photograph of two girls on a shore; the locket is Evie's most persistent tether to the world of the living.
A sepia photograph, larger than the one in the locket, of two girls standing on a marshy shore. Someone, long ago, wrote a name on the back in faded ink: 'Evie.'

Noah Whitcomb, an elderly neighbor who remembers the house and the girl named Evie. He is stubborn and blunt, keeps to his own property across the lane, and provides a few key facts about the past — but not all of them.

arguments.logline: When Mara returns to her childhood house to settle her mother's affairs, a walnut mirror in the attic keeps showing a girl who isn't her — a ghost tethered to a brass locket and to being seen — and the more Mara tries to prove it's a trick, the more the house's reflections conspire to make her the only one who can remember Evie, perhaps at the cost of herself.

scenes.intent: Establish atmosphere, Mara's practical, grieving voice, and the house as a character. Have Mara force open the attic, discover the walnut mirror and a trunk with the brass locket and the faded photo. End with the first impossible thing: the mirror's reflection shows a second figure — a girl at the far end of the attic — when no one else is present. The scene should make the reader feel unease and plausibility (drafts, memory, grief as explanation) while leaving the apparition unresolved.

Escalate the logic of the haunting. Mara runs tests: covers the mirror, looks into other reflective surfaces, notes timing and consistency. The mirror's reflection behaves differently (it remembers the house as it was; the girl's clothing doesn't match present-day). Mara opens the locket, reads the name 'Evie' on the back of the larger photo, and hears a child's voice through the mirror — not quite a sound, more like a thought-pressing. She tries to record it, to get proof, and something in the house reacts physically (a chair shifts, a cold imprint on the drywall). End with Mara deciding to talk to Noah — there is a problem that is at least historical and traceable.

Mara visits Noah to get facts that anchor the ghost to a real person and a time. Noah confirms an Evie Ashford vanished/drowned decades earlier; he gives a fragmentary memory that suggests jealousy, the marsh, and a small funeral. This scene supplies the ghost's plausible motive (wanting to be remembered/named) and a concrete place (the low tide mudflats where the photo was taken) to which a tether might be returned. Mara returns to the house with a plan: either bury the locket where Evie drowned, or smash the mirror — the choices both follow from the world rules. This scene must keep the logic tight: Noah supplies one verifiable archival detail (newspaper clipping, name on old gravestone, or a date) that Mara can check.

Climax and payoff. Mara sets out to perform the chosen test (return the locket to the shore at low tide and speak the name aloud while the reflection watches, or confront the mirror and shatter it). The ghost escalates: reflections elsewhere show Mara's family watching; the house tries to keep her. The scene ends with a logically consistent, terrifying outcome — not a cheap twist. Two plausible, internally consistent resolutions are foreshadowed so that whichever the writer chooses (liberation at cost, or Mara becoming the new tether), the scene will feel earned. The scene should be visceral: marsh mud, salt-stiff hair, the sound of glass underfoot, and the mirror's last image burning itself into Mara's mind.

world_rules: The ghost is anchored to objects of memory (the brass locket and the faded photograph). Those objects, while intact, allow the ghost to fix and replay a moment of its life via reflective surfaces.

Reflections are the ghost's active domain: mirrors and other clear reflections can show the past as a layer over the present and can carry limited sensory impressions (voice, cold, a touch through the glass), but they do not automatically permit the ghost to 'step' into the physical world.

A ghost cannot leave the property unless it has a physical tether placed on it in the outside world (for example, the locket buried at the marsh). Returning a tether to the place tied to the tether can either sever the ghost's hold (freeing it) or strengthen the ghost's claim, depending on whether the act is done as a named remembrance or as an attempt to hide/forget it.

Physical destruction of the mirror severs the reflection-channel but does not by itself destroy the ghost; it redirects the ghost's attention to other reflections and, if done without the remembering ritual, can enrage the ghost and make it more dangerous.

Naming matters: saying the ghost's name aloud while the tether and a reflection are present is a ritual act that changes the balance — it can either grant the ghost a 'witness' to be satisfied by (calming it) or allow it to take stronger hold of the namer if the namer's attention falters or they lie to themselves.

I had to force the attic open.

Decision: the mirror leaned against the far wall beneath a small west window, trunks stacked in a line under the rafters. Decision: as a child I had never been told about Evie — the name was missing from our family stories.

The hatch stuck on the second pull. My hands were already raw from hauling boxes downstairs and answering questions I did not have the patience for, so I used the crowbar the estate agent had left in the garage and pried the thing up in two impatient breaths. A soft cold rose out of the dark as if the house had been holding its breath; the attic smelled of old oilcloth and wood that remembered damp. Nobody had been up here in years and, absurdly, the floorboards were almost clean: dustless in that particular way of places you avoid and thus never disturb.

Light came through a small west window in a narrow beam that slid across trunks and splinters of packing crate. The mirror was where I said I would picture it: tall, walnut-framed and full-length, the glass slightly warped so the rafters bent as if they were breathing. It stood propped against the far wall, catching the slant of the afternoon. The trunks were stacked along the left-hand side under the rafters, one on top of another like a spine of brittle leather.

The largest trunk yielded without drama. The leather flaked where my fingers pressed, and the brass catches sighed and opened. Inside, on a pad of yellowing tissue, lay a small, tarnished brass locket on a fragile chain and, beside it, a larger sepia photograph folded carefully in a moth-eaten handkerchief. I did not gasp. I turned things over like inventory — list, label, bag, move on.

The locket was colder than the air. I pried it open with my thumbnail and found a tiny photograph of two girls pressed flat inside. I had to hold the picture up to the light to make out faces: wind-stung cheeks, skirts blown at odd angles. On the back of the larger photograph, when I unfolded it, someone had written a single name in faded ink: Evie.

I said it aloud to the empty rafters because saying a thing aloud is how I make things real for myself. "Evie," I said, and the sound felt too small for the attic.

I turned toward the mirror as if to check how I looked — hair out of place, the same hands I had used to split the hatch — and the reflection made me do a double-take. There, at the far end of the attic where shadow pooled behind the trunks, the glass held a second figure: a girl standing a little way from the trunks, head tilted as if listening. The rest of the attic, the boards under my boots, the crowbar by the hatch, showed no one. I tested it the way you test a trick: I stepped left, then right, blinked, even leaned so my shoulder cut the angle of the light. The girl did not move in unison; she stayed at the far end, a pale, steady shape in the glass.

I told myself a dozen sensible things. Old frames can double images. Mirrors warp. Grief makes you see family in the wrong places. I was tired and practical and there were boxes to label. Still, I kept the locket in my palm and I could feel my pulse in the chain. The girl in the mirror had no label I could read, only the posture of a person waiting, and that waiting felt like an accusation.

I closed my fingers around the locket and put it in my pocket because the sensible thing was to put important things somewhere safe. Then I stood with the hatch open and listened to the house settle, and the mirror kept the girl.
